section.title: Warning Against Idolatry
section.sectionRationale: This chapter addresses internal threats to covenant loyalty, a prophet, a family member, or an entire city enticing Israel to idolatry, prescribing severe measures bound tightly to Israel's unique covenant nationhood that must never be read as warrant for violence against dissenting belief in any later era.
section.thesis: Moses warns that even a prophet with real signs, a beloved family member, or an entire city can become an instrument of enticement to idolatry, and Israel must love the LORD supremely enough to reject and purge such enticement decisively, however painful, though these commands are bound to Israel's unique role as a covenant nation and are never a warrant for violence against dissenting belief today.
section.frameNote: Three movements: false prophets who lead astray, even with real signs; enticement from a beloved family member or closest friend; and an entire city that has gone astray after careful investigation.

verses.text: If a {{nabi|prophet}} or dreamer of dreams arises among you and proclaims a sign or wonder to you,
and if the sign or wonder he has spoken to you comes about, but he says, “Let us follow other gods (which you have not known) and let us worship them,”
you must not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the LORD your God is {{nasah|testing}} you to find out whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul.
You are to follow the LORD your God and fear Him. Keep His commandments and listen to His voice; serve Him and hold fast to Him.

Such a prophet or dreamer must be put to death, because he has advocated rebellion against the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery; he has tried to turn you from the way in which the LORD your God has commanded you to walk. So you must purge the evil from among you.

units.label: Even a brother or closest friend

verses.text: If your very own brother, or your son or daughter, or the wife you embrace, or your closest friend secretly entices you, saying, “Let us go and worship other gods” (which neither you nor your fathers have known,
the gods of the peoples around you, whether near or far, whether from one end of the earth or the other),
you must not yield to him or listen to him. Show him no pity, and do not spare him or shield him.
Instead, you must surely kill him. Your hand must be the first against him to put him to death, and then the hands of all the people.
Stone him to death for trying to turn you away from the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
Then all Israel will hear and be afraid, and will never again do such a wicked thing among you.
If, regarding one of the cities the LORD your God is giving you to inhabit, you hear it said
that wicked men have arisen from among you and have led the people of their city astray, saying, “Let us go and serve other gods” (which you have not known),
then you must inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly. And if it is established with certainty that this abomination has been committed among you,
you must surely put the inhabitants of that city to the sword. {{cherem|Devote to destruction}} all its people and livestock.

And you are to gather all its plunder in the middle of the public square, and completely burn the city and all its plunder as a whole burnt offering to the LORD your God. The city must remain a mound of ruins forever, never to be rebuilt.
Nothing devoted to destruction shall cling to your hands, so that the LORD will turn from His fierce anger, grant you mercy, show you compassion, and multiply you as He swore to your fathers,
because you obey the LORD your God, keeping all His commandments I am giving you today and doing what is right in the eyes of the LORD your God.

nabi.gloss: Prophet, one who speaks on behalf of God. This chapter warns that the office and even accurate signs do not authenticate a message; a prophet's words must always be tested against what the LORD has already revealed.

nasah.gloss: To test, to try, to prove. Here God Himself is described as permitting a test through a false prophet's fulfilled sign, exposing whether Israel's love for Him is genuine and supreme above every other claim on their loyalty.

cherem.gloss: To devote irrevocably to destruction. Applied here to an apostate Israelite city, showing that the severity once reserved for Canaanite idolatry in chapter 7 applies equally within Israel itself when covenant loyalty is abandoned for other gods.

basic.context: Moses warns Israel that enticement to idolatry can come from surprising and painful sources, a prophet performing real signs, a beloved family member, or an entire city, and commands that such enticement be rejected and purged decisively rather than tolerated because of its source's credibility or closeness.
basic.hermeneutics: This is one of Deuteronomy's hardest passages and needs honest, careful reading: it prescribes capital measures bound tightly to Israel's unique identity as a covenant nation-state, where loyalty to the LORD was inseparable from national and civil identity. It gives no warrant whatsoever for the church or any government to use violence against religious dissent or unbelief today.
basic.originalLanguages: Even a genuine nabi, prophet, whose sign comes true is to be rejected if his message contradicts the LORD; the fulfilled sign itself functions as a nasah, test, of whether Israel's love for God is supreme. An apostate city is subject to cherem, the same total devotion to destruction earlier commanded against Canaanite idolatry, now applied within Israel itself.
basic.typology: Jesus warns that false prophets and false messiahs will perform great signs and wonders to deceive even the elect if possible, Matthew 24:24, directly echoing this chapter's principle that a real sign does not validate a message contrary to God's word.
basic.christ: Where Israel's civil order used the sword to purge enticement to idolatry, the New Testament calls the church to purge evil from its fellowship through spiritual discipline, not violence, 1 Corinthians 5:13, and entrusts final judgment on all deception entirely to Christ at His return, 2 Thessalonians 2:8-10.
basic.god: God is jealous for exclusive, supreme love from His people, so much so that He allows even a false prophet's fulfilled sign to function as a genuine test of that love; yet the chapter closes by naming mercy, not mere severity, as God's ultimate purpose for His people's obedience.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 24:24 warns of false messiahs and prophets performing great signs to deceive. 2 Thessalonians 2:9-10 describes the lawless one's false wonders. 1 Corinthians 5:13 calls the church to purge evil from its own fellowship through discipline, not violence. 2 Thessalonians 1:6-10 entrusts final judgment on evil entirely to Christ.
basic.oneStory: This chapter names how seriously God takes the exclusivity of His people's love, even when enticement comes from credible or beloved sources. The New Testament carries this same seriousness forward into the church's call to discern truth, exercise loving discipline, and trust final judgment on all deception entirely to Christ.

context.literary:
The chapter is built from three cases, each opened by the same Hebrew word for "if" in verses 1, 6 and 12. Each case quotes the tempter's actual words, and the words hardly change: "Let us follow other gods," verse 2, "Let us go and worship other gods," verse 6, "Let us go and serve other gods," verse 13. Each quotation is followed by the same aside, "which you have not known," verses 2, 6 and 13. The repetition is the point. However different the messenger, the message is always the same invitation, and Moses wants Israel to recognise it by its content rather than by the voice that carries it.

The three cases widen in scope and change in visibility. The prophet acts in public with a sign everyone can see. The relative works "secretly," verse 6, inside the household. The city is known only by report, "you hear it said," verse 12, so the third case alone requires a formal inquiry. The penalty grows with the scope: death for the prophet and the relative, and for the city the full cherem once reserved for Canaan.

The word "listen" frames the chapter. Israel must not listen to the prophet, verse 3, but must listen to the LORD's voice, verse 4. They must not listen to the relative, verse 8, and the chapter ends with Israel obeying, literally listening to, the voice of the LORD, verse 18. Two motive clauses recall the exodus, verses 5 and 10, grounding the command in redemption rather than raw authority.

In the Hebrew Bible the chapter division falls one verse earlier, so that 12:32, "do not add to it or subtract from it," stands as the heading of the chapter. That placement suits the argument. Chapter 12 guarded the place and manner of worship; chapter 13 guards its object. Many interpreters also notice that the laws of chapters 12 to 26 roughly follow the order of the Ten Commandments, and on that reading chapters 12 and 13 expound the first two, no other gods and no idols.
context.historical:
Moses speaks in the land of Moab, east of the Jordan, Deuteronomy 1:5, to a generation about to settle among the cities and shrines of Canaan. The danger he anticipates is not an army but a conversation: a respected voice, a spouse, a neighbouring town that has quietly taken up the gods of the land. Baal and the fertility gods promised rain and harvest, and a people turning from wilderness manna to farming would feel the pull of gods who claimed to govern the seasons, as the story of Baal of Peor had already shown, Numbers 25:1-3.

Prophecy and dreams were ordinary channels of revelation in the ancient Near East. Letters from the city of Mari on the Euphrates report prophets and dreamers bringing messages from the gods to the king, and Israel itself knew that the LORD could speak "in a dream," Numbers 12:6. So a dreamer with a fulfilled sign would carry real weight. Egypt had already taught Israel that signs could be counterfeited, for Pharaoh's magicians "did the same things by their magic arts," Exodus 7:22.

The chapter also reads like a clause from a royal loyalty oath. Ancient treaties bound vassals to report and act against any word of rebellion, and an Assyrian loyalty oath from the reign of Esarhaddon in the seventh century BC names prophets, ecstatics and oracle seekers, as well as a man's own brothers, sons and daughters, as possible sources of sedition. Deuteronomy uses the same shape for a covenant with a divine King. To entice Israel to other gods is to "advocate rebellion," verse 5, treason against the Sovereign who redeemed them.

The procedure for the city reflects Israel's legal practice. Investigation must be thorough, verse 14, and elsewhere a death sentence required two or three witnesses, Deuteronomy 17:6. The ruined city left as a mound, verse 16, would have been a familiar sight: ancient towns were rebuilt on their own debris, and a tel left permanently empty was a visible sentence.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a cluster of laws in Deuteronomy about true and false worship. Deuteronomy 17:2-7 applies the same procedure to an individual idolater, with the same insistence on thorough investigation and the same line, "you must purge the evil from among you." Deuteronomy 18:15-22 then adds a second test for prophets: a prophet whose word fails is not from the LORD. Chapter 13 supplies the harder case, the prophet whose word succeeds but whose message leads away from God, so that together the two chapters say a true prophet must be both accurate and faithful.

Israel's history shows the law's concerns playing out. The Levites had already gone "against his son and his brother" for the LORD's sake at the golden calf, Exodus 32:29. An old prophet deceives a man of God with a claimed angelic message in 1 Kings 13:18. Elijah executes the prophets of Baal, 1 Kings 18:40. Jeremiah condemns Hananiah and Shemaiah because each "preached rebellion against the LORD," Jeremiah 28:16 and 29:32, borrowing the very phrase of verse 5. Zechariah 13:3 pictures a day when a false prophet's own father and mother will refuse to spare him, an echo of verses 6 to 9.

The New Testament keeps the test while changing the sword. Jesus warns that false Christs and false prophets "will appear and perform great signs and wonders," Matthew 24:24 and Mark 13:22. Paul describes the lawless one's "power, sign, and false wonder," 2 Thessalonians 2:9, and Revelation's second beast deceives by signs, Revelation 13:13-14. John tells believers to "test the spirits," 1 John 4:1. Paul quotes the purge formula for church discipline, 1 Corinthians 5:13, and applies the logic of verse 3 to apostles and angels alike: a contrary gospel is under a curse whoever preaches it, Galatians 1:8-9. Jesus Himself was accused of being a deceiver, John 7:12 and Matthew 27:63, the charge this chapter defines, yet He came in His Father's name, John 5:43.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to settle one question before they cross the Jordan: what finally has authority over them? His answer is that the LORD's already spoken word outranks every competing voice, however impressive or dear. A miracle does not outrank it, verse 3. A marriage does not outrank it, verse 6. The majority in a whole town does not outrank it, verse 13.

He also wants them to understand why. The chapter twice names the LORD as the One "who brought you out of the land of Egypt," verses 5 and 10. Loyalty is the fitting answer to redemption, and so turning to other gods is not a private spiritual preference but ingratitude and treason against the Redeemer.

Finally he wants them to interpret temptation rightly. A fulfilled sign that points away from God is not a reason to doubt God; it is a test through which He finds out "whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul," verse 3, the language of Deuteronomy 6:5. The positive list of verse 4, follow, fear, keep, listen, serve, hold fast, shows the goal is not suspicion for its own sake but undivided love. And the chapter ends by promising mercy, compassion and growth to a people who obey, verses 17 and 18, so that the severity serves life rather than destruction.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is genuinely prescriptive law, not narrative, but it is law for Israel as a nation under the LORD's direct kingship in the land. Its penalties belong to that covenant order, in which the community of worship and the civil state were one body. Jesus says His kingdom "is not of this world," John 18:36, rebukes disciples who wanted to call down fire on a village that rejected Him, Luke 9:54-55, and Paul says the church does not "wage war according to the flesh," 2 Corinthians 10:3. When Paul quotes the formula "expel the wicked man from among you," he applies it to exclusion from the church's fellowship, and he adds that "God will judge those outside," 1 Corinthians 5:12-13.

The church has not always read the chapter this way. In the sixteenth century it was appealed to in defending the execution of heretics, most famously in the case of Michael Servetus at Geneva, a use that most Christians now regard as a grave misreading. What carries over is the principle beneath the penalty: every message is judged by its faithfulness to God's word, love for God must outrank every human tie, and a community of faith must deal seriously with teaching that leads people away from Him.

debates.question: How should Christians read the death penalty prescribed here for enticing others to idolatry, even applied to family members or entire cities?

views.label: Bound to Israel's unique theocratic covenant
views.case: Israel functioned uniquely as a covenant nation in which loyalty to the LORD was at once religious and civil identity; these penalties belong to that specific national administration and are never extended to the church or any modern state, which wields no equivalent mandate, John 18:36 and 2 Corinthians 10:3-4. Paul's use of verse 5 in 1 Corinthians 5:13 shows the transposition: exclusion from fellowship replaces execution.

views.label: An enduring picture of the seriousness of apostasy, not a transferable legal precedent
views.case: Some read this passage primarily as urgent, vivid language underscoring how seriously God takes covenant betrayal, using the strongest sanctions available within Israel's specific civil order, without intending these particular penalties as a pattern for any other era or nation. The weight falls on the call to love God supremely, verse 3, rather than on the mechanics of punishment.

views.label: Civil penalties that still bind governments
views.case: A minority, notably in the twentieth century movement called theonomy, argued that the Mosaic civil penalties remain the standard of justice for every nation. Most Christian traditions reject this, because it ignores the change of covenant, the church's calling to suffer rather than coerce, and the New Testament's explicit handling of these texts.

debates.bearing: The first two readings agree this text gives no warrant whatsoever for the church or any government to inflict violence for religious dissent or unbelief today, and the third fails to account for how the New Testament itself applies the chapter. God's people are redirected to persuasion, loving discipline within the church, and final judgment entrusted entirely to Christ, 2 Thessalonians 1:6-10 and Romans 12:19.

debates.question: How can a false prophet's sign actually come true, and in what sense is the LORD behind it?

views.label: God sovereignly permits deception as a test
views.case: Verse 3 says plainly that the LORD is testing Israel. Other texts speak the same way: a lying spirit is permitted to entice Ahab through his prophets, 1 Kings 22:22-23, and God sends a powerful delusion on those who refused the love of the truth, 2 Thessalonians 2:10-11. On this view God does not lie, but He rules even deception and uses it to expose what is in the heart, as He did in the wilderness, Deuteronomy 8:2.

views.label: The power comes from spiritual evil
views.case: Pharaoh's magicians matched some of Moses' signs, Exodus 7:22, and the New Testament attributes the signs of the lawless one to 'the working of Satan,' 2 Thessalonians 2:9, and those of the second beast to deceptive power, Revelation 13:13-14. On this reading the sign is real but its source is hostile, and the test lies in whether Israel will be impressed by power or held by the word.

views.label: The sign may be ordinary foresight or coincidence
views.case: Some note that the text does not call the sign miraculous and that a shrewd prediction or lucky guess could also 'come about,' verse 2. The law then covers every case, whatever the mechanism, because it judges the message rather than the method.

debates.bearing: The chapter does not answer the mechanical question, and it does not need to. Its concern is that no sign of any kind can authorise a call to other gods. The first two views fit together well: evil may supply the power, but the LORD rules over it and turns it into a test of love.

study.originalLanguages:
"Signs and wonders," ot and mofet, is the vocabulary of the exodus. Moses uses the pair for what the LORD did "in Egypt, before your eyes," Deuteronomy 4:34, and the book closes by saying no prophet ever did "all the signs and wonders" Moses did, Deuteronomy 34:11. When verse 1 gives the false prophet "a sign or wonder," the text deliberately puts exodus language in the mouth of a man calling Israel back into another kind of slavery. The test is therefore sharp: the enticer borrows the very credentials of the God he wants them to leave.

The aside "which you have not known" uses yada, the verb of personal, covenant acquaintance rather than mere information. Israel has known the LORD by experience, in redemption and provision. The other gods are strangers, "newly arrived gods, which your fathers did not fear," Deuteronomy 32:17, and the same phrase marks apostasy in the blessing and curse of Deuteronomy 11:28.

The verb for "entices" in verse 6 is sut in its causative stem, to incite or instigate. Its uses elsewhere are telling: Jezebel "incited" Ahab to evil, 1 Kings 21:25; Satan "incited" David to take the census, 1 Chronicles 21:1; and in Job 2:3 the LORD says to Satan, "you incited Me against him." It describes pressure applied by someone close and trusted, which is exactly the setting of verses 6 to 11.

The charge in verse 5, "he has advocated rebellion," is literally "he has spoken sarah," a word for turning aside or revolt. Jeremiah reuses the exact charge against Hananiah and Shemaiah, "you have preached rebellion against the LORD," Jeremiah 28:16 and 29:32, showing that the prophets consciously read their opponents through this chapter.

Two uses of dabaq, to cling, frame the obedience of the chapter. Verse 4 commands Israel to "hold fast" to the LORD, the verb of Genesis 2:24, where a man is "united" to his wife, and of Deuteronomy 10:20 and 30:20. Verse 17 then uses the same verb negatively: nothing devoted to destruction "shall cling to your hands." Israel must cling to God and let nothing of the idol cling to them.

The "wicked men" of verse 13 are literally "sons of beliyya'al," sons of worthlessness, the phrase used for the men of Gibeah, Judges 19:22, and for Eli's sons, 1 Samuel 2:12. By New Testament times Belial had become a name for the devil, as in 2 Corinthians 6:15.

The burning of the city is described as a kalil, a "whole burnt offering," verse 16, the word used of Samuel's offering in 1 Samuel 7:9, and the ruin is to be a tel olam, a "mound of ruins forever," the phrase used of Ai in Joshua 8:28. As the BSB footnote on verse 15 explains, cherem means handing something over to the LORD, whether by destruction or as an offering. The Septuagint regularly renders it with anathema, the word Paul uses in Galatians 1:8-9 when he says that anyone preaching a contrary gospel is "under a curse."

typology.type: The true prophet tested by his message, Deuteronomy 13:1-5 with 18:15
typology.fulfillment: Deuteronomy sets two tests for a prophet: his word must come true, 18:22, and it must lead to the LORD, 13:3. Moses promised a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear, Deuteronomy 18:15, and Peter applies that promise to Jesus, Acts 3:22-23. Jesus meets both tests perfectly. His signs are 'miracles, wonders, and signs, which God did among you through Him,' Acts 2:22, and His teaching 'comes from Him who sent Me,' John 7:16. He does not draw people from the God of the exodus; whoever has seen Him has seen the Father, John 14:9. Where the type falls short, Christ surpasses it: He is not only faithful to the word but is the Word.

typology.type: Purging the evil from among you, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Israel removed the enticer by death so that the evil would not spread through the camp. Paul quotes the same formula for the church, 'Expel the wicked man from among you,' 1 Corinthians 5:13, but the means change from the sword to exclusion from fellowship, and the aim becomes restoration, 'so that his spirit may be saved,' 1 Corinthians 5:5. The escalation is inward: the Spirit purifies a people from within, and the final removal of evil belongs to Christ at His coming, 2 Thessalonians 1:7-10. The type falls short because Israel's purge could remove an offender but could not change a heart.

typology.type: Loyalty to God above the closest human bond, verses 6 to 11
typology.fulfillment: Verse 6 names brother, son, daughter, 'the wife you embrace' and the friend who is as your own soul, and still insists that love for the LORD must come first. Jesus makes the same claim for Himself: 'Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me,' Matthew 10:37, and He quotes Micah 7:6 to warn that a disciple's enemies may be in his own household, Matthew 10:36. The escalation is striking, since Jesus claims the loyalty Deuteronomy reserves for God alone. The type falls short in its method: disciples are not told to strike their families but to take up a cross, Matthew 10:38.

typology.type: The city devoted to the LORD as a whole burnt offering, verses 15 to 17
typology.fulfillment: An apostate city became cherem, handed over wholly to God in judgment, and left as a permanent ruin. The Old Testament itself looks for a day when this will end: of the restored Jerusalem Zechariah says, 'never again will there be an utter destruction,' Zechariah 14:11, using the same word. The New Testament shows how that happens. Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13, and in the city to come 'no longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3. The type falls short because the ruined city could only bear its own judgment; Christ bore the judgment of others.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the question of authority. Its whole burden is that no voice may lead Israel away from the LORD who brought them out of Egypt, however strong its credentials. Jesus stepped into exactly that setting. He did signs, and He also made claims no prophet had made, so that some said, "He deceives the people," John 7:12, and the Pharisees asked the temple officers, "Have you also been deceived?" John 7:47. After His death the chief priests still called Him "that deceiver," Matthew 27:63. In effect they were judging Him by Deuteronomy 13.

The Gospels answer the charge on the chapter's own terms. The test of verse 3 is not the sign but the direction of the message, and Jesus insists that His direction is toward the Father: "My teaching is not My own. It comes from Him who sent Me," John 7:16. He says, "I have come in My Father's name," and warns that others will come in their own name and be received, John 5:43. He even invites His hearers to judge Him by His works, "If I am not doing the works of My Father, then do not believe Me," John 10:37. Far from leading Israel to gods they had not known, He is the Son in whom the God of the exodus is seen, John 14:9.

Christ also takes up the chapter's warning and aims it at the future. Matthew 24:24 promises false Christs with "great signs and wonders," and in Matthew 7:22-23 He foresees people who prophesied and worked miracles in His name and yet never knew Him. Signs without faithfulness are still worthless. John's instruction to "test the spirits," 1 John 4:1, is followed by a test centred on Christ: the spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, 1 John 4:2.

The chapter leads to Christ, too, by the love it demands. Verse 3 asks for love with all the heart and soul, and verse 6 places that love above spouse, children and dearest friend. Jesus claims that same place for Himself, Matthew 10:37 and Luke 14:26, which only makes sense if He shares the identity of the LORD whose love the chapter guards.

Finally, the chapter's severity finds its resolution at the cross rather than its copy in the church. The disciples who wanted fire on a Samaritan village were rebuked, Luke 9:54-55. Instead of devoting rebels to destruction, Christ became a curse for them, Galatians 3:13. The church still purges evil from its fellowship, 1 Corinthians 5:13, but final judgment on every deceiver is His, when the lawless one is slain "with the breath of His mouth," 2 Thessalonians 2:8. Care is needed here: the chapter is not a hidden picture of Jesus in every detail. Its link to Him runs through the New Testament's own use of its tests, its warnings and its call to undivided love.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He has already spoken, and that His spoken word is the fixed point by which every later voice is measured. The chapter assumes a revelation Israel already possesses, "the way in which the LORD your God has commanded you to walk," verse 5. God is not reinventing Himself each time a new prophet arises. He is consistent, and so His people can test new claims against what He has said, Isaiah 8:20.

He is sovereign even over deception. Verse 3 does not say the false prophet slipped past God's notice. It says, "the LORD your God is testing you." The same God who led Israel through the wilderness "to test you in order to know what was in your heart," Deuteronomy 8:2, rules the circumstances in which His people are tempted. That does not make Him the author of the lie; Scripture elsewhere holds both that deceiving powers are real and that they operate only within His rule, 1 Kings 22:22-23 and 2 Thessalonians 2:11. The purpose is disclosure: He wants to find out whether Israel's love is real, and to let Israel find out as well.

He is jealous for love, not merely for obedience. The chapter's measure is love "with all your heart and with all your soul," verse 3, and its list of duties in verse 4 is warmly relational: follow, fear, keep, listen, serve, hold fast. The jealousy of Exodus 20:5 is the jealousy of a husband for a wife, not the insecurity of a rival deity. That is why the enticement is compared to leaving the God "who redeemed you from the house of slavery," verse 5.

He is also just and careful. The third case forbids action on rumour. Israel must "inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly," verse 14, and act only if it is "established with certainty." God's severity is never careless. The same God who takes apostasy with deadly seriousness requires due process before judgment.

The chapter holds severity and mercy together in a way that can feel uncomfortable. The same paragraph that devotes a city to destruction ends by promising that the LORD "will turn from His fierce anger, grant you mercy, show you compassion, and multiply you," verse 17. The word for compassion there comes from racham, the root associated with a mother's womb. The judgment is meant to clear the way for the mercy, and the mercy is tied to the oath "He swore to your fathers," so that God's faithfulness to Abraham stands behind the whole chapter.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to a love that is not easily impressed. Signs, charisma, family pressure and social consensus all have real weight, and God does not pretend otherwise. But the God who redeemed His people deserves the whole heart, and worship that is truly His will cling to Him and to His word, even when every other voice says, "Let us go."

crossReferences.note: The companion test for prophets. Deuteronomy 18 says a prophet whose word fails has spoken presumptuously; chapter 13 says a prophet whose word succeeds but leads to other gods must still be rejected. Together they teach that accuracy is necessary but never sufficient. A true prophet speaks what comes true and what draws Israel to the LORD.

The same law applied to an individual idolater. The case must be investigated thoroughly, two or three witnesses are required, and the witnesses' hands are first in the execution, as in 13:9. It shows that the severity of chapter 13 was surrounded by strict safeguards against rumour and false accusation.

The LORD led Israel through the wilderness to test them 'in order to know what was in your heart.' Deuteronomy 13:3 uses the same testing language for a false prophet's sign. Hardship in the desert and a dazzling sign in the land are both occasions God uses to reveal whether His people's love is real.

Jeremiah tells the prophet Hananiah he will die because he has 'preached rebellion against the LORD,' the very charge of Deuteronomy 13:5. Hananiah's message sounded hopeful and patriotic, yet it contradicted God's word. His death that same year shows the prophets applying this chapter within Israel's history.

Zechariah foresees a day when God removes idols and false prophets, and a false prophet's own father and mother refuse to let him live. The picture deliberately recalls Deuteronomy 13:6-9, where even the closest family bond must not shield someone who leads others away from the LORD.

Jesus warns that false Christs and false prophets 'will appear and perform great signs and wonders that would deceive even the elect, if that were possible.' He applies the principle of Deuteronomy 13:1-3 to the last days: signs cannot validate a message that draws people away from the true Christ.

Jesus says He brings a sword that divides households, quoting Micah 7:6, and that whoever loves father, mother, son or daughter more than Him is not worthy of Him. The loyalty that Deuteronomy 13:6 places above spouse and child is claimed by Jesus as due to Himself.

Paul says that even if he or 'an angel from heaven' preached a contrary gospel, that one should be under a curse. Like Deuteronomy 13:3 he refuses to let the messenger's credentials override the message. The word for curse is the Greek word the Septuagint uses for cherem.

Paul quotes the purge formula of Deuteronomy, 'Expel the wicked man from among you,' and lists the idolater among those the church must not keep in fellowship. He adds that God will judge those outside. The formula moves from the civil sword to the church's discipline of its own members.

The lawless one comes with 'every kind of power, sign, and false wonder,' deceiving those who 'refused the love of the truth.' As in Deuteronomy 13:3, God's rule stands over the deception, for He sends a delusion on those who rejected the truth. Love for truth is the safeguard in both passages.

The risen Christ rebukes the church in Thyatira for tolerating a woman who 'calls herself a prophetess' and leads His servants to idolatry. It is Deuteronomy 13 inside the church: a prophetic voice enticing to false worship. The remedy Christ gives is repentance and His own judgment, not the church's sword.

John tells believers to 'test the spirits' because many false prophets have gone out, and he gives a test centred on confessing Jesus Christ come in the flesh. It is the New Testament form of Deuteronomy 13: every spiritual claim is measured by its faithfulness to what God has revealed.

study.oneStory:
Deuteronomy 13 stands at a hinge in the Bible's story. God has created a people for Himself, redeemed them from Egypt and bound them to Himself by covenant at Sinai. The whole purpose of that redemption was a relationship of undivided love, Deuteronomy 6:4-5. From the garden onward, the great threat to that relationship has come as a voice questioning God's word, and Genesis 3:1 began with just such a voice. This chapter anticipates the same voice speaking with Israel's own accent: a prophet, a spouse, a town.

What follows in Israel's history shows how real the danger was. Judges records generation after generation turning to the Baals, Judges 2:11-13. Jezebel's prophets fill the northern kingdom, 1 Kings 18:19, and Jeremiah contends with prophets who speak peace when there is no peace. Israel does not purge the evil from among it; instead the evil takes root until the nation itself is sent into exile. In a sense the cherem of verses 15 to 17 falls on Jerusalem, and Micah had already warned that Jerusalem would "become a heap of rubble," Jeremiah 26:18.

Yet the story does not end in ruins. Zechariah foresees idols and false prophets removed from the land, Zechariah 13:2, and a Jerusalem where "never again will there be an utter destruction," Zechariah 14:11. The way to that future runs through the Prophet like Moses, whose word proved true and whose message led to the Father, and who took the curse upon Himself, Galatians 3:13.

In the present age the church lives between the warning and the fulfilment. False prophets still arise, Matthew 24:24 and 2 Peter 2:1, and believers must test the spirits and discipline their own fellowship. But the church does not wield the sword; it waits for the Lord who will destroy the lawless one at His coming, 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

The new creation completes what this chapter could only defend. Babylon, the great deceiver of the nations, falls, Revelation 18:23, the false prophet is thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 19:20, and in the city of God there is no longer any curse, Revelation 22:3. There God's people will not need to be warned against other gods, because they will see His face and worship Him alone, Revelation 22:4. The love Deuteronomy 13 guarded with such severity will at last be whole.

quiz.q: According to verse 3, why might the LORD allow a false prophet's sign or wonder to actually come true?

options.text: To test whether Israel truly loves the LORD with all their heart and soul.
options.note: Verse 3 gives this exact reason for God permitting such a test.

options.text: Because false prophets always have real power equal to God's.
options.note: The text frames this as a test God permits, not evidence of equal or rival power.

options.text: It never actually happens; false signs never come true.
options.note: Verse 2 explicitly considers the case where the sign does come about.

options.text: No reason is given.
options.note: Verse 3 gives an explicit theological reason.

quiz.q: What does Moses say should happen if a close family member secretly entices someone to worship other gods (vv.6-9)?

options.text: They must not yield or show pity, and must be the first to put that person to death, without shielding them.
options.note: Verses 8-9 state this severe requirement explicitly.

options.text: They should be reported to the elders for a fine.
options.note: The text prescribes a far more severe response than a fine, capital punishment carried out by the community.

options.text: They should be forgiven immediately without any consequence.
options.note: The passage explicitly forbids showing pity or sparing the person, the opposite of automatic forgiveness.

options.text: Nothing is instructed regarding family members.
options.note: Verses 6-9 address this situation directly and at length.

quiz.q: What must happen before an entire city can be judged for turning to idolatry (v.14)?

options.text: Israel must inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly to establish with certainty that the report is true.
options.note: Verse 14 requires exactly this careful process of verification.

options.text: A single unverified rumor is sufficient for immediate judgment.
options.note: The text requires thorough investigation, the opposite of acting on unverified rumor.

options.text: No verification process is needed at all.
options.note: Verse 14 explicitly requires careful investigation before any judgment.

options.text: Nothing about investigation is mentioned.
options.note: Verse 14 addresses this process explicitly.

quiz.q: What happens to a whole city confirmed to have turned to other gods (vv.15-16)?

options.text: Its people and livestock are devoted to destruction and the city is burned completely, never to be rebuilt.
options.note: Verses 15-16 describe this severe, total judgment.

options.text: Only its leaders would be punished.
options.note: The judgment described extends to the whole city, not only its leaders.

options.text: The city would simply be fined heavily.
options.note: The judgment described is total destruction, far more severe than a fine.

options.text: No punishment for the city is described.
options.note: Verses 15-16 describe the punishment in explicit detail.

quiz.q: What is the ultimate purpose given for these severe measures against enticement to idolatry (v.18)?

options.text: So that Israel would obey the LORD, keep His commandments, and do what is right, and He would show them mercy.
options.note: Verses 17-18 name mercy and covenant faithfulness as the ultimate purpose.

options.text: So that Israel could seize more territory and wealth.
options.note: No such purpose is named; the stated goal is obedience leading to God's mercy.

options.text: So that other nations would fear and worship Israel instead of God.
options.note: The purpose named is Israel's own obedience and God's mercy toward them, not the nations' worship of Israel.

options.text: No purpose is given for these measures.
options.note: Verses 17-18 give an explicit purpose.

questions: Moses warns that even someone with real spiritual gifts or apparent signs can lead people away from God if their message contradicts His revealed word. How do you currently test what you hear, even from gifted or persuasive people, against Scripture itself?

This chapter names even a beloved family member as a potential source of enticement away from God. Is there a relationship in your life where love has quietly made you unwilling to name a harmful spiritual influence honestly?

This passage belongs to Israel's unique covenant nationhood and gives no warrant for violence toward anyone today; instead the church is called to loving discipline, trusting final judgment to Christ. Where do you need to release judgment of someone into God's hands rather than trying to control or punish them yourself?

Before judging an entire city, Israel was required to investigate thoroughly rather than act on rumor. Where might you be tempted to judge a situation quickly rather than seeking out the full truth first?

The purpose behind these hard commands was ultimately mercy, obedience leading to God's compassion (v.18). How does viewing even God's hardest commands as ultimately aimed at mercy change how you read a passage like this one?

translationNotes.note: This passage's logic, that God may permit a real sign to accompany a false message as a test of love, is echoed directly by Jesus in Matthew 24:24 regarding false messiahs and prophets in the last days.

'Purge the evil from among you' is a recurring formula throughout Deuteronomy's legal sections, marking the seriousness with which covenant-breaking sin was to be treated within Israel's specific civil order.

'A whole burnt offering' likens the apostate city's total destruction to a sacrificial offering, framing this severe judgment within Israel's own worship categories rather than as an act of mere warfare.
